criteria.name: Q1 Quality attributes
criteria.reasoning: Chooses performance and availability, justified with lunch peak, 4.2 s p95 and payment outage. Both scenarios contain source, stimulus, artefact, environment, response and measurable response measures. Full six-part form.

evidence.quote: Performance and availability matter most: 900 orders arrive in the lunch hour, the 4.2 s p95 makes students abandon their orders
Response measure: the p95 response time is under 1.5 s and no requests are dropped.
Response measure: menu p95 stays under 2 s, under 0.1% of non-payment requests fail, and ordering works again within 1 minute of the provider recovering.

criteria.name: Q2 Architectural style
criteria.reasoning: Clear modular monolith recommendation. Trade-offs are scenario-specific: five-developer team vs service overhead, and known single-VM/20-minute downtime vs rewrite cost. Downside acknowledged.

evidence.quote: I recommend a modular monolith (modules: orders, menu, payments, outlets) rather than a microservices rewrite for the next 12 months.
The downside I accept is that modules cannot be scaled independently and a bug in one module can still crash the whole process.

criteria.name: Q3 Availability calculation
criteria.reasoning: All three parts correct with working: series product 99.30%, 5.0 h downtime, active-active payment pair 99.9975%, end-to-end 99.80%, 1.5 h downtime. Rounding matches requested precision.

criteria.name: Q4 Resilience pattern
criteria.reasoning: Names circuit breaker, explains closed/open/half-open mechanism, applies it to the 25-minute payment hang, and gives tuning and fallback drawback.

evidence.quote: The Circuit Breaker pattern [2] would have contained the failure.
Drawback: nobody can pay while it is open, so a fallback is needed.

criteria.name: Q5 Consistency and availability
criteria.reasoning: Chooses AP for menu with Redis cache and CP for payments with rejection/idempotency. CAP is stated correctly and both choices are justified by user impact.

evidence.quote: The CAP theorem says that during a partition a system must give up either consistency or availability
Each order request carries an idempotency key, so a retry does not create a second charge.

criteria.name: Q6 Architecture decision record
criteria.reasoning: ADR has specific Context, Decision and Consequences. Positive and negative consequences are both present, including operational load and at-least-once duplicate handling.

evidence.quote: Context: After an order is paid, the application calls the outlet's tablet synchronously and waits for the reply.
Consequences (negative): The queue is one more component for five developers to run and monitor.

criteria.name: Communication and format
criteria.reasoning: Required headings appear in order; answers are at or under 150 words; terminology is precise; IEEE-style references are present.

evidence.quote: [1] L. Bass, P. Clements, and R. Kazman, Software Architecture in Practice, 3rd ed.

overall: Excellent submission: all six answers are technically sound, calculations correct, and format compliant. Minor omission: no explicit assumptions section beyond the 30-day month statement.

feedback.summary: You submitted a strong, complete response: all six questions are answered, Q3 calculations are correct, and your Q1 scenarios are fully six-part with measurable measures. Q2's modular monolith recommendation is well justified, and Q4–Q6 apply patterns and CAP precisely. The only gap is an explicit assumptions section beyond the 30-day month statement. Keep this standard.

In Q1, keep the measurable response measures; for future work, add a one-line note on why other attributes (e.g., security, modifiability) were ranked lower to make the prioritisation even more defensible.

For Q2 and Q6, continue naming scenario-specific trade-offs and both positive and negative consequences; to secure top marks every time, explicitly link each consequence back to the five-developer team or the 20-minute outage.
